content: The guidelines aim to empower and impact various groups, including residents of communities where schistosomiasis is endemic, visitors and tourists to these areas, distributors of medicines during preventive chemotherapy, health ministry officials at district or administrative levels, national neglected tropical disease (NTD) program managers and coordinators, national pharmacovigilance agencies, national medicine regulatory authorities, ministries of education and the environment, manufacturers of preventive chemotherapy medicines, and donor organizations supporting schistosomiasis control and elimination programs. The guidelines are based on the best available evidence as of 2021, but the evidence base for many questions remains limited and subject to change. Updates will be made as new evidence emerges. Summary of Recommendations: 1. Annual Preventive Chemotherapy in Endemic Communities with ≥10% Prevalence The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends annual preventive chemotherapy with a single dose of praziquantel at ≥75% treatment coverage for all age groups (from 2 years old, including adults, pregnant women after the first trimester, and lactating women). This aims to control schistosomiasis morbidity and work toward eliminating the disease as a public health problem. Implementation Considerations: Prevalence is defined as the percentage of individuals infected with any Schistosoma species in the target population. The strategy does not vary by Schistosoma species. A 10% prevalence threshold is based on parasitological microscopy using stool or urine samples. Point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen tests can also be used, with a 30% prevalence by this test equating to 10% by microscopy. Routine monitoring of treatment coverage and impact (via population-based surveys after five rounds of chemotherapy or mid-term evaluations after three rounds) is essential. Expanded programs increase the theoretical risk of drug resistance, necessitating ongoing monitoring of praziquantel efficacy. Preventive chemotherapy is appropriate for preschool-aged children (≥2 years), with individual clinical consideration for those <2 years. Pediatric formulations (e.g., oral disintegrating tablets) are under development, but crushed praziquantel in soft food may be used if necessary. High treatment coverage is critical and may require incentivizing local drug distributors and public health awareness campaigns to address concerns about adverse events. 2. Communities with <10% Prevalence WHO suggests two approaches based on programmatic objectives and resources: Continuing preventive chemotherapy at the same or reduced frequency to interrupt transmission. Using a clinical test-and-treat approach instead of population-wide preventive chemotherapy. Implementation Considerations: Close epidemiological monitoring (e.g., sentinel site surveys or mid-term evaluations every three years) is necessary, especially in areas previously ≥10% prevalence or with a history of preventive chemotherapy. 3. Biannual Preventive Chemotherapy in High-Prevalence Communities with Poor Response to Annual Treatment In endemic communities with ≥10% prevalence that show inadequate response to annual treatment (defined as <33% reduction in prevalence after two years of annual chemotherapy with ≥75% coverage), WHO suggests biannual treatment. Implementation Considerations: Biannual treatment should prioritize areas with baseline prevalence ≥50% in school-aged children or persistent hotspots. Routine monitoring of treatment coverage and impact is essential before transitioning to biannual treatment. Biannual programs require a larger global supply of praziquantel and should space treatments approximately six months apart. 4. Access to Treatment for All Infected Individuals WHO recommends that health facilities provide praziquantel treatment to all infected individuals, regardless of age, including pregnant women (excluding the first trimester), lactating women, and children <2 years (based on clinical judgment). Implementation Considerations: Pregnancy status should be assessed discreetly, with urine-based pregnancy tests used if necessary. Pediatric formulations are under development, but crushed praziquantel in soft food may be used for individual cases. 5.g., water engineering and snail control with molluscicides), and behavioral change interventions to reduce schistosomiasis transmission. Implementation Considerations: WASH interventions provide modest benefits for schistosomiasis but also reduce risks for other infectious diseases. Behavioral change interventions should begin alongside preventive chemotherapy programs. Coordination between schistosomiasis control and WASH programs is essential, with mapping and sharing of epidemiological and WASH coverage data to prioritize endemic areas. Snail control should be prioritized in persistent hotspots and integrated with mass treatment campaigns to accelerate morbidity control and elimination goals. A larger, cost-effective global supply of molluscicides and skilled snail control workers will be required. Additional Notes: Schistosomiasis is a parasitic disease caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma. It is transmitted when humans or infected animals contaminate freshwater with excreta containing parasite eggs, which hatch in water. The larval forms (cercariae) penetrate human skin during contact with infested water, developing into adult worms in the bloodstream. Preventive chemotherapy, the core public health strategy, involves large-scale treatment with praziquantel to reduce infection levels and prevent morbidity. The guidelines emphasize the importance of integrating WASH interventions, snail control, and behavioral change strategies to achieve long-term elimination of schistosomiasis. Monitoring and evaluation, including the use of sensitive diagnostic tools, are critical to assess program impact and guide adjustments in strategy.
